---
title: "Crash Severity and Missing Data in Pennsylvania"
subtitle: "How missing-data treatments bias a crash model, and which factors make rural crashes fatal or seriously injurious"
author:
  - "Jonathan Wilson"
---

This project analyzes Pennsylvania Department of Transportation (PennDOT) crash records in two parts:

1. **Missing-data treatments.** The same {{< var md.n_rows >}} crashes come with gaps that are
   *missing at random* (MAR) in one file and *missing not at random* (MNAR) in another. We compare
   mean imputation, median imputation and complete-case removal against a reconstructed
   "best-available truth", and measure how much each treatment biases a logistic regression.
2. **Rural crash severity.** Using first principles and a simple statistical filter, we select ten
   features and build a logistic regression that identifies crashes in which someone is killed or
   seriously injured, interpreted for **rural roads**.

::: {.callout-note}
## Headline findings
- **Complete-case removal is the most biased treatment**, especially under MNAR: it drops the more
  severe crashes and roughly doubles coefficient error. Mean imputation is the least biased simple
  method; median imputation turns every missing yes/no value into "no".
- **On rural roads, aggressive driving contributes the most severe crashes** (present in 9 of 11),
  while **motorcycles are the most dangerous single factor** (odds ×4.6). Impairment and speeding each
  raise the odds about 2.4×. Deer strikes are four times more common on rural roads but were never severe.
- The final 10-feature model reaches a rural ROC AUC of {{< var rs.auc_rural >}} and finds about
  41% of severe rural crashes, from only {{< var rs.n_rural_severe >}} severe rural cases.
:::

![](assets/figures/fig-rs-odds-ratios.png){fig-alt="Odds ratios with 95% bootstrap intervals for the ten selected crash factors. Motorcycle, impaired driver and speeding raise the odds of a severe crash; rear-end, distracted, deer-related and dark conditions lower it."}

## Data

Crash records and the data dictionary come from the PennDOT Open Data Portal (crash data dictionary,
version 06-26). The extracts used here (`features.xls`, `MAR_ex1.xls`, `MNAR_ex1.xls`) were provided
for coursework.
